rule: Reuse existing code and utilities by factoring or subclassing instead of copying or reimplementing them.
Do not add a parameter where a constant, default, automatic behaviour or existing storage will do; keep the parameter count down.
Generic features belong in shared libraries usable by every vehicle, not in one vehicle directory or vehicle-specific code.
Optional features need their own enable macro (defined 0/1 in the library _config.h, listed in build_options.py) and every dependent declaration, call and member must be compiled out when it is off.
Use singletons only where exactly one instance is intended; backends are not singletons.
Every parameter needs complete documentation: description, Range, Units, Values/Bitmask, matching the code.
Prefer early returns over nested conditionals.
Add pre-arm checks for configurations that would silently misbehave, make them specific, and put them in the shared or owning library.
Never block or busy-wait in the main thread; do waits and slow work asynchronously via a state machine or other thread.
Model driver and feature state explicitly in one state machine, and update state only where the action actually succeeds.
Use elapsed-time differences from a stored start, not added timestamps.
Minimise public interface; use const, references and accessors appropriately.
Bound loops and buffers, check pointers and return values, validate external or user-supplied values, and guard domain maths.
Avoid unnecessary or static allocation, handle allocation failure, allocate only when the hardware or feature is present, and keep memory initialisation safe.
Prefer the simplest design; do not add complexity, options or mechanisms for small or hypothetical gains.
Initialise members in-class and do not zero-initialise needlessly.
Use enum class and switch without default so the compiler flags new values.
Avoid constructs that cost flash for little gain (bitfields, packed structs, virtuals, copies).
Periodic work goes in the normal scheduler table at a rate chosen by measured CPU cost, and expensive calls are kept out of hot paths.
Define macros always, test with #if, wrap tunable defaults in #ifndef and keep defines out of headers.
Principles that fit no repeated theme.
Comments must be accurate, concise, say why not what, and appear once in the right place.
Follow commit conventions: correct subsystem prefix, commits that compile, no fixups or accidental changes.
Do not add features to minimal-flash boards or minimal peripheral firmware; do not use blanket feature stripping as the way to recover flash.
Changes must be tested on real hardware and relevant variants, not just compiled.
New or niche features default to off and are enabled only on the boards and vehicles that need them.
Names must describe what the thing actually is or does, be positive and consistent.
Do not break existing users, GCS clients, APIs or stored configuration; behaviour changes need impact assessment.
Tests must restore state and parameters (try/finally, context push/pop) and clean up what they load.
Tests must assert what they claim, cover edge cases, be cheap and robust, and actually exercise the changed code.
Bring in third-party code as a submodule or isolated directory and do not modify the vendored source.
Hardware-backed and new features must be runnable and tested in SITL.
Remove unused, broken or obsolete code rather than keeping it.
Keep PRs and commits to a single issue and split out unrelated, refactor or easily-mergeable changes.
Every PR needs a description stating the problem, impact and what testing was done.
Put logic and state in the class or library that owns them, avoid roundabout data paths, and do not duplicate decisions across callers.
Data shared between threads needs proper protection (WITH_SEMAPHORE, consistent snapshots, bounded waits), and primitives must be used correctly.
Use internal_error for impossible states and genuine misuse so they surface in logs, not for external input or harmless cases.
Avoid adding new state flags or variables when the source of truth already exists; do not repurpose existing ones.
Never change or overload the meaning of an existing parameter; add a new one.
Use a 32-bit _OPTIONS bitmask for orthogonal options, with clear precedence and no reuse of bits.
State the flash, CPU and RAM cost of a change, and justify it, especially for boards with little flash.
Libraries log their own data with their own log bit, not vehicle or unrelated code.
Log bandwidth is finite; quantify and limit added log output.
Log messages: stable short fields, new fields at the end, documented, no duplicate messages.
Avoid changing user-set parameters from code; if needed use set_and_save_ifchanged, make it opt-in, and use set() so the GCS is informed.
Follow hwdef conventions: shared .inc files, generic defaults from hwdef rather than board hacks, tooling kept generic.
Respect release timing: no large or risky changes late, backports via separate PRs, and note user-visible changes.
Keep GCS status text low volume, rate-limited, via GCS_SEND_TEXT, and actionable.
Fix the problem at its root, in the layer that decides the behaviour, rather than papering over it downstream.
Respect layering: lower layers must not call up, and callers use the abstraction layer (AHRS, SRV_Channels, library owner) instead of reaching into backends or internals.
New boards and build variants need their registrations, READMEs and build-script entries; keep build output structure working.
Failsafe and safety logic must fail in the safe direction, handle combined and on-ground cases, and not disable or be bypassed by unrelated logic.
Use appropriately sized fixed-width types, unit suffixes and sizeof/constants instead of literals.
Verify no-op refactors by identical compiler output rather than by reasoning.
Renamed or re-encoded parameters need a dated conversion that preserves user settings.
Validate parameter values and handle runtime changes safely.
Hardware- and platform-specific code goes through AP_HAL and HAL setup hooks, not shared libraries or vehicle code.
Sensor driver changes must be robust (timeouts, glitches, variants), consistent with sibling backends, and not break other chip variants.
Log timestamps must be monotonic and reflect the data time.
Shared changes must be tested on every affected vehicle type.
New code and fixes need regression tests that fail before and pass after.
Fixes and behaviour changes need evidence: logs, repro steps, measurements and a correct explanation.
Authors must review and trim AI-generated code, comments and replies themselves.
Home, EKF origin and position are distinct concepts and must be handled and named accordingly.
Arming checks must have no side effects; state changes belong in arm().
Factor repeated conditions into a named predicate method.
Protocol code should use clear decoders and packed structs, be bounds-safe, and be robust to garbage input.
Autotests wait on a defined condition rather than a fixed delay.
Scripting bindings should not break existing APIs, should return ready-to-use values with frames, and need examples.
EKF/AHRS and flight-state-dependent changes are high risk: keep them minimal, backend-agnostic, plumb data through DAL, and test across vehicles and edge cases.
Code in mainline is a permanent burden: it must be well designed, justified and not narrow special-purpose.
Avoid duplicated documentation that will go stale; point to one canonical source.
Parameter names and display names are specific, lead with the feature name, use standard terms and keep prefixes short.
Keep vehicle code thin and consistent; give mode hooks defaults and call them polymorphically, and require overrides via pure virtual.
Avoid default arguments with a single caller or where callers must choose.
Report failures clearly to the user through an appropriate channel.
Default changes need care: use set_default, keep exceptions explicit, and weigh impact on existing users.
Libraries detect faults; the vehicle code decides and takes the action, and checks needing vehicle context live in vehicle code.
Changes to hwdef scripts, DMA or shared HAL code must be checked against all boards (configure_all.py) and test-built.
Risky or controversial changes go through a dev call or discussion before code review.
Never reuse or move an AP_GROUPINFO index; new parameters go at the end and optional ones in optional objects.
Control-law, gain-scaling and filter changes can destabilise tuned aircraft and need frequency/time-domain justification and A/B evidence.
Changes to core math helpers need unit tests of boundary values, consistent zero/sign semantics and flight testing.
New code must be built by at least one board in CI.
